concepts.title: Lambda Expressions & Functional Interfaces
concepts.description: A lambda expression is a compact block of behavior with no name and no type of its own. It becomes meaningful once it is matched against a functional interface, an interface with one abstract method. That matching, plus a strict rule about which local variables a lambda may use, makes lambdas both powerful and occasionally surprising.
learningObjectives: Define what a functional interface is and explain why it must have exactly one abstract method.
Write a lambda expression and explain how both its parameter types and its target interface are inferred from context.
Name and use at least four of the standard java.util.function interfaces: Function, Predicate, Consumer, and Supplier.
Use each of the four kinds of method references and explain when each one applies.
Explain why a lambda can read but not reassign a captured local variable, and connect this to the 'effectively final' rule.
Contrast a lambda's this with an anonymous inner class's this.

sections.heading: Functional Interfaces: An Interface With Exactly One Job
Lambda Syntax and Target Typing
sections.body:
A lambda expression has the shape `(parameters) -> body`, where the body is either a single expression (its value becomes the return value) or a `{ }`-braced block of statements (which needs `return` if it produces a value). Parameter types are almost always omitted and inferred; parentheses around a single parameter can be dropped too.

```java
(String name) -> "Hello, " + name             // explicit parameter type
name -> "Hello, " + name                       // type inferred, parens optional for one param
(a, b) -> a + b                                // multiple params, types inferred
(a, b) -> { int sum = a + b; return sum; }     // block body needs an explicit return
```

This trips people up at first: a lambda expression, by itself, **has no type**. Its type comes from the context it is used in, which Java calls **target typing**. The same lambda text can implement different functional interfaces depending on where it is assigned or passed.

```java
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("running");            // target type: Runnable
Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("running"));  // same-shaped lambda, target type inferred from Thread's constructor parameter
```

Both lambdas are the same text, `() -> System.out.println("running")`. The first is matched against `Runnable`'s `run()` because that is the declared type of `r`; the second is matched against whatever functional interface `Thread`'s constructor parameter expects (also `Runnable` here). The *context*, not the lambda text, does the matching.

sections.heading: The Standard Toolkit: java.util.function
sections.body:
Instead of writing a new one-method interface every time you need to pass around a small piece of behavior, `java.util.function` provides general-purpose functional interfaces for the common shapes:

- `Function<T, R>`: one method, `R apply(T t)`, takes a `T`, produces an `R`.
- `Predicate<T>`: one method, `boolean test(T t)`, takes a `T`, returns true/false.
- `Consumer<T>`: one method, `void accept(T t)`, takes a `T`, returns nothing (pure side effect).
- `Supplier<T>`: one method, `T get()`, takes nothing, produces a `T`.

```java
Function<String, Integer> length = s -> s.length();
Predicate<String> isBlank = s -> s.trim().isEmpty();
Consumer<String> print = s -> System.out.println(s);
Supplier<String> greeting = () -> "Hello!";

System.out.println(length.apply("hi"));   // 2
System.out.println(isBlank.test("   "));  // true
print.accept(greeting.get());              // prints "Hello!"
```

Several of these interfaces also have `default` methods for composing them without writing a new lambda: `Predicate.and`, `.or`, and `.negate()` combine predicates logically, and `Function.andThen` and `.compose` chain two functions, differing in which runs first (the exercises below try this). Recognizing the four shapes (takes X, returns Y; takes X, returns boolean; takes X, returns nothing; takes nothing, returns Y) covers a large fraction of the lambdas you will write.

Variable Capture: Effectively Final, and this Inside a Lambda

examples.title: Target Typing: The Same Lambda Literal, Two Different Interfaces
examples.explanation: The same lambda text, (a, b) -> a + b, is written twice and means something different each time because of the variable it is assigned to. The first targets Calculator, a custom functional interface whose single abstract method is compute(int, int), so the lambda implements compute. The second targets BinaryOperator<Integer> (a standard interface whose single method is apply(T, T)), so the same text now implements apply, working on boxed Integer values instead of raw ints. That is target typing: the lambda has no fixed type, and the compiler decides what it implements from the type it is assigned to or passed as.

examples.title: The Four Kinds of Method References, Side by Side
examples.explanation: Each method reference stands in for a lambda that only forwards to one existing method. Integer::parseInt is a static method, so parse.apply("42") is the same as calling Integer.parseInt("42"). log::add refers to the add method of one SPECIFIC existing List (log), so append.accept(...) always adds to that same list. String::toUpperCase is different: no String object is named anywhere, and whatever argument upper.apply(...) receives becomes the object toUpperCase() is invoked ON, which is why it works as a Function<String, String> with one parameter. ArrayList::new is a constructor reference: newList.get() is the same as writing new ArrayList<>() inline, useful wherever a Supplier of a fresh instance is needed.

examples.title: Effectively Final Capture: What Compiles, and the Mutable-Counter Workaround
examples.explanation: threshold is assigned once and never reassigned, so it is effectively final and can be captured without the final keyword. The commented-out block would not compile: total += n inside the lambda reassigns total, and captured locals may not be reassigned anywhere in their scope, so javac reports that total must be final or effectively final. The AtomicInteger version works because runningTotal as a variable is assigned once (effectively final), so capturing it is legal. What changes across calls is the state inside the object it points to (addAndGet mutates that object), not the reference held in the local variable. This is the standard idiom when a lambda has to accumulate mutable state across invocations.

misconceptions.description: A lambda expression has a fixed type of its own -- for example, x -> x * 2 'is a Function'.
misconceptions.clarification: A lambda expression has no type in isolation. It acquires one only when matched against a target functional interface determined by its context: an assignment's declared type, a method parameter's declared type, or a cast. The same lambda, x -> x * 2, could implement Function<Integer, Integer>, UnaryOperator<Integer>, or any custom functional interface with a single int-to-int abstract method, depending on where it is written. 'The type of a lambda' only makes sense once you ask 'assigned to what?'

misconceptions.description: A lambda captures local variables the way closures do in languages like JavaScript or Python -- it keeps a live, mutable connection to the variable, seeing any later reassignment.
misconceptions.clarification: Java lambdas may only capture local variables that are effectively final: never reassigned after their initial assignment. The compiler rejects any attempt to capture a reassigned variable, which avoids the live-mutable-capture ambiguity those other languages accept. When a lambda needs shared, changing state, the idiomatic workaround is to capture a reference to a mutable container, such as a one-element array or an AtomicInteger / AtomicReference, whose reference stays effectively final while its contents change through method calls.
misconceptions.fact: Java lambdas may only capture local variables that are effectively final: never reassigned anywhere in their enclosing scope after their initial assignment.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to count how many times run() is called, but it fails to compile. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: Look at what the lambda body does to count. Is count assigned to more than once anywhere in this method?
Local variables captured by a lambda must be effectively final: never reassigned after their initial assignment, anywhere in their enclosing scope.
Replace the plain int with a mutable container whose reference itself never changes, such as an AtomicInteger, and call a method on it to both increment and read the value.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original fails to compile because count++ inside the lambda reassigns count, so it is not effectively final, and every local captured by a lambda must be. The lambda might run later or elsewhere, and there would be no single answer to 'which value did it capture' if the variable kept changing. The fix replaces the int with an AtomicInteger: the local variable count is assigned once (to the new AtomicInteger(0)), which satisfies the rule, while incrementAndGet() mutates the state inside that one object instead of reassigning the variable. The two calls to r.run() print 1, then 2.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? Pay close attention to the difference between andThen and compose.
hints: f.andThen(g) means 'run f first, then run g on f's result': for combinedA, that means doubleIt runs first.
f.compose(g) means 'run g first, then run f on g's result'. The order is the REVERSE of andThen. For combinedB, that means addTen runs first.
Compute combinedA.apply(5) step by step: doubleIt(5) first, then addTen on that result. Then do the same for combinedB, but with the two steps swapped.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 20, then 30. combinedA (andThen) computes doubleIt(5)=10, then addTen(10)=20. combinedB (compose) computes addTen(5)=15, then doubleIt(15)=30.
exercises.solutionExplanation: doubleIt.andThen(addTen) applies doubleIt FIRST, then feeds the result into addTen. combinedA.apply(5) computes doubleIt(5) = 10, then addTen(10) = 20, so it prints 20. doubleIt.compose(addTen) is the reverse: it applies addTen FIRST, then feeds the result into doubleIt. combinedB.apply(5) computes addTen(5) = 15, then doubleIt(15) = 30, so it prints 30. Both chain the same two functions and differ in which runs first: andThen reads left to right in the order you wrote the calls, while compose runs its argument first and the original function second.

assessments.prompt: Why must a functional interface have exactly one abstract method, no more and no fewer?
options: It's an arbitrary restriction the JDK team chose to keep interfaces simple; it has no real technical necessity.

Java requires this only for interfaces explicitly annotated @FunctionalInterface; unannotated interfaces can have any number of abstract methods and still be used with a lambda, with the compiler choosing between them by looking at the parameter names in the lambda.
Having more than one abstract method would make the interface too slow to call at run time.

A lambda's body is just an expression or block of statements with no method name attached -- the compiler needs exactly one unambiguous abstract method signature on the target interface to know what that body is implementing.
assessments.explanation: A lambda expression carries no method name, so matching it against an interface requires exactly one abstract method for the compiler to bind the lambda's parameters and body to. With two or more, there would be no way to know which one the body is meant to implement. The “It's an arbitrary restriction the JDK team…” option is wrong: this is a technical necessity, not an arbitrary style choice. The “Having more than one abstract method would…” option is wrong: this has nothing to do with runtime performance. The “Java requires this only for interfaces explicitly…” option is wrong: @FunctionalInterface is optional documentation plus a compiler check, not what makes the rule apply. Any interface with exactly one abstract method can be a lambda's target type whether or not it carries the annotation, and adding the annotation to an interface with two or more abstract methods is a compile error.

assessments.prompt: Explain to someone who understands methods and interfaces, but has never used lambdas, what a lambda expression actually is, how target typing determines what it implements, and why it can only read (not reassign) certain local variables from its surroundings.
assessments.modelAnswer: A lambda expression is a compact, inline way of writing the single method body of a functional interface implementation (an interface with exactly one abstract method), without a full named class or an anonymous class. Something like name -> "Hello, " + name just describes 'take one parameter, produce this value' and has no fixed type on its own. Target typing gives it meaning: wherever the lambda is written (assigned to a functional interface variable, passed to a functional interface parameter, or cast), the compiler uses that context to decide which interface's abstract method it implements and checks that the lambda's parameter count and body fit that signature. The same lambda text can implement different interfaces in different places, so there is no 'type of this lambda' independent of its context. As for variable capture: a lambda body is allowed to read local variables and parameters from its enclosing scope, but only ones that are 'effectively final': assigned exactly once and never reassigned anywhere afterward in that scope, even if the final keyword isn't written. This exists because a lambda can be invoked later than, and separately from, the method call that created it: stored in a field, handed to another thread, called back after the original method has already returned, and if the captured variable were allowed to keep changing, there would be no single well-defined answer for which value the lambda should see. Rather than trying to define some complicated live-capture semantics, Java disallows capturing anything that changes, and pushes anyone who needs shared, mutable state accessed from inside a lambda toward capturing a reference to a mutable container object instead: the reference stays effectively final even while the object's own internal state changes through its own methods.

assessments.prompt: Function<String, Integer> len = String::length; What does this method reference actually mean, given that no specific String object appears anywhere in the expression?
options: It's an instance method reference on an arbitrary object of a given type: whatever single argument is passed to len.apply(...) becomes the object that length() is actually called on, exactly equivalent to writing s -> s.length().

This fails to compile, because an instance method can never be referenced without explicitly specifying a receiver object, so the line would need to be rewritten as a call on one specific String that has already been created and assigned to a variable.
It calls length() on a fixed, hidden String object that the JVM creates internally every time len.apply(...) is called.
It treats length as if it were a static method of String, calling it with no receiver object at all.
assessments.explanation: This is the third method-reference form: when the referenced method is an instance method and no object is named, the incoming parameter becomes the receiver. Function<String, Integer> takes one String and returns an Integer, and s.length() fits that shape, with s supplied at call time as len.apply(s). The “It calls length() on a fixed, hidden…” option invents a hidden object that doesn't exist. The “This fails to compile, because an instance…” option is wrong: this exact form (an instance method reference on an arbitrary object of a type) is one of the four standard, fully legal method reference forms. The “It treats length as if it were…” option is wrong because length() is an instance method on String, not a static one; the method reference works because the argument becomes the receiver, not because the method is static.

assessments.prompt: List<Runnable> tasks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { int current = i; tasks.add(() -> System.out.println(current)); } Why does this compile, when capturing the loop variable i directly -- tasks.add(() -> System.out.println(i)); -- would not?
options: current and i are actually the same variable under the hood, so there's no real difference -- both versions would compile identically.

current is a brand-new local variable, freshly declared and assigned exactly once within each loop iteration, so it's effectively final for that iteration's lambda; i, by contrast, is reassigned by the loop's own update step (i++) on every iteration, which disqualifies it from being effectively final.
This fails to compile as written too, because ArrayList cannot hold a list of lambdas.
Lambdas can only capture variables declared with the exact keyword final, and current happens to satisfy that requirement while i does not.
assessments.explanation: Each pass through the loop body declares a fresh current and assigns it exactly once, so from the lambda's point of view inside that one iteration, current is never reassigned anywhere in its scope: effectively final. i, however, is a single variable shared across every iteration, and the loop's update clause reassigns it on every pass, which makes it fail the effectively-final test regardless of which iteration's lambda tries to capture it. The “current and i are actually the same…” option is wrong: current and i are different variables, with different values captured across iterations, which is why the copy-into-current pattern is a standard idiom. The “Lambdas can only capture variables declared…” option overstates the rule: effectively final variables don't need the final keyword at all, only the never-reassigned property. The “This fails to compile as written too…” option is a fabricated, unrelated claim; ArrayList holds references of any type, lambdas included.

assessments.prompt: class Handler { private String label = "handler"; Runnable makeLambdaRunnable() { return () -> System.out.println(this.label); } Runnable makeAnonymousRunnable() { return new Runnable() { public void run() { System.out.println(this.label); } }; } } What is true about each method?
options: Both fail to compile, because this can never be referenced inside any implementation of a functional interface.
makeAnonymousRunnable() compiles fine and makeLambdaRunnable() fails, because lambdas are never allowed to reference this under any circumstance.

makeLambdaRunnable() compiles fine -- a lambda introduces no instance or this of its own, so this.label correctly refers to the enclosing Handler's field; makeAnonymousRunnable() fails to compile, because the anonymous class genuinely creates its own object with its own this, which has no field named label, requiring Handler.this.label to reach the enclosing instance instead.
Both compile fine and print "handler", because this always refers to the enclosing Handler instance inside both a lambda and an anonymous class.
assessments.explanation: A lambda body behaves as if it were written inline in the enclosing code, it introduces no new this at all, so this.label inside the lambda resolves to Handler's own label field as it would anywhere else in makeLambdaRunnable. An anonymous class, by contrast, creates a distinct object of its own, with its own this, and that anonymous Runnable object has no field named label, so this.label inside its run() method fails to compile (there being no such member to resolve to); reaching the enclosing Handler's label from inside the anonymous class requires the more verbose Handler.this.label. The “Both compile fine and print "handler"…” option ignores this, difference. The “Both fail to compile, because this can…” option is wrong: this is used constantly and correctly inside lambdas, referring to the enclosing context. The “makeAnonymousRunnable() compiles fine and makeLambdaRunnable() fails…” option reverses which one has the problem.

concepts.title: The Stream API: map, filter, reduce, and collect
concepts.description: A Stream describes a pipeline over a source of data. Lazy intermediate operations like map and filter only build up that description, and nothing runs until a terminal operation like collect or reduce pulls elements through the whole chain, once.
learningObjectives: Describe the three-part shape of a stream pipeline: a source, a chain of intermediate operations, and a terminal operation.
Explain why intermediate operations are lazy and only actually execute once a terminal operation is invoked.
Use map, filter, sorted, and distinct to transform a stream, and explain the difference between stateless and stateful intermediate operations.
Use reduce with an identity value and a combining function to fold a stream's elements into a single result.
Use collect with common Collectors (toList, toMap, groupingBy, joining) to gather stream results into a concrete structure.
Explain why a stream can only be consumed once, and predict the exception that results from reusing one.

sections.heading: The Shape of a Stream Pipeline: Source, Intermediate, Terminal
sections.body:
A `Stream` does not store elements the way a `List` does. It describes a computation over a source of data. Every pipeline has the same three parts: a **source** (a collection's `.stream()`, `Stream.of(...)`, `IntStream.range(...)`), zero or more **intermediate operations** (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`), and exactly one **terminal operation** that produces a non-stream result and ends the pipeline (`collect`, `reduce`, `forEach`, `count`, `anyMatch`, `findFirst`).

```java
List<String> names = List.of("Amy", "Ben", "cara", "Dev", "amy");

List<String> result = names.stream()          // source
    .filter(n -> n.length() <= 3)              // intermediate
    .map(String::toUpperCase)                  // intermediate
    .distinct()                                // intermediate
    .sorted()                                  // intermediate
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toList());  // terminal
```

Intermediate operations always return another `Stream`, which is what allows them to be chained fluently one after another; a terminal operation returns something else: a `List`, an `int`, a `boolean`, an `Optional`. And once it runs, the pipeline is finished.

sections.heading: Laziness: Nothing Runs Until the Terminal Operation Is Invoked
map, filter, and the Stateless vs Stateful Distinction
sections.body:
`filter(Predicate<T>)` keeps the elements that satisfy a condition and discards the rest; `map(Function<T, R>)` transforms every element into a new value, possibly of a different type, one-to-one. Both are **stateless**: deciding what to do with one element never requires knowing anything about another.

`sorted()` and `distinct()` are **stateful**. `sorted()` cannot know an element's final position until it has seen every other element, and `distinct()` must remember every element it has emitted to recognize a later duplicate. In practice, stateful operations generally buffer more of the stream at once, behave differently (and sometimes worse) on very large or infinite streams, and interact with parallel streams in ways that `map` and `filter` don't have to worry about.

```java
List<Integer> result = java.util.stream.Stream.of(5, 3, 5, 1, 3, 2)
    .distinct()   // [5, 3, 1, 2] -- must remember what it's already seen
    .sorted()     // [1, 2, 3, 5] -- must see everything before it can order anything
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toList());
```

sections.heading: reduce: Folding Everything Into One Value
sections.body:
`reduce` combines a stream's elements pairwise into one result. The two-argument form, `reduce(identity, BinaryOperator<T>)`, takes a starting value (the **identity**, which is also the result for an empty stream) and a function that combines two values into one, applied repeatedly across the stream.

```java
int sum = java.util.stream.Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4)
    .reduce(0, (a, b) -> a + b);   // 0+1=1, 1+2=3, 3+3=6, 6+4=10
System.out.println(sum);           // 10
```

There is also a one-argument overload, `reduce(BinaryOperator<T>)`, with no identity to fall back on. Since an empty stream then has no sensible answer, it returns `Optional<T>` instead of `T`, which forces the caller to consider the empty case. Use `reduce` to fold elements into one summary value of the *same* type (a sum, a maximum, a concatenation). To build a *different* kind of result (a `List`, a `Map`, a grouped structure), `collect` is almost always the more idiomatic tool, covered next.

sections.heading: collect and Collectors: Building an Actual Result Structure

examples.title: A Full Pipeline: filter, map, sorted, collect
examples.explanation: filter(w -> w.length() > 3) keeps only words longer than 3 characters, dropping "fig" (length 3); map(String::toUpperCase) then transforms each surviving word to uppercase, one element at a time; sorted() orders the resulting strings alphabetically; and collect(Collectors.toList()) is the terminal operation that finally triggers all of this and gathers the result into a List. Nothing in this pipeline executes until collect is reached: filter, map, and sorted each just add a step to the pipeline's description, in the exact order written, and elements are pulled through that whole chain only once the terminal operation demands a result.

examples.title: Laziness Made Visible
examples.explanation: The first pipeline calls .map(...) with no terminal operation. It compiles, and running it prints no "mapping ..." lines, because nothing pulls elements through it: the statement is a no-op. The second pipeline is the same except for .collect(Collectors.toList()), a terminal operation, and that addition makes it run, printing "mapping amy", "mapping ben", "mapping cara" as each element is pulled through map, before the final "result = [AMY, BEN, CARA]". The map() lambda is unchanged between the two versions. What differs is whether anything downstream asks for a result. (The terminal operation here is collect: with count() on a List source, Java 9 and later can return the size without running map at all.)

examples.title: reduce for a Single Summary Value vs collect for a Structured Result
examples.explanation: reduce(0, Integer::sum) folds the stream of individual word lengths down into a single int: 0 is the identity (also the correct answer for an empty stream), and Integer::sum combines two lengths at a time into a running total, ending at 19. This is the right tool here because the desired result (one summary number) is fundamentally a single value of the same general kind (a number) being accumulated across the stream. collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length)), by contrast, isn't folding anything down to one value: it's building a different KIND of structure, a Map from each distinct length to the list of words that have that length. groupingBy applies String::length to each word to compute its key, and automatically buckets each word into a list under that key: the kind of structured, multi-shaped result that reduce is a poor fit for and collect handles.

misconceptions.description: Calling .filter(...) or .map(...) on a stream processes all the elements immediately, the same way calling a method on a List would.
misconceptions.clarification: Intermediate operations like filter and map are lazy: calling them only records a step in the pipeline, and no element is processed at that moment. Nothing runs until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count, and so on) is invoked, and then elements are pulled through the ENTIRE chain, typically one at a time. One visible consequence is that a chain of intermediate operations with no terminal operation compiles fine and does nothing at run time, a no-op rather than an error.

misconceptions.description: A stream variable can have a terminal operation called on it more than once, the same way you can call .size() on a List as many times as you want.
misconceptions.clarification: A Stream can be traversed exactly once. The moment a terminal operation runs, that stream is considered consumed (the specification calls this 'operated upon or closed'), and any further operation attempted on that same stream reference (even a completely different terminal operation) throws IllegalStateException at run time: 'stream has already been operated upon or closed'. To run the same or a different pipeline again, you need a fresh stream, typically by calling .stream() again on the original underlying collection or source, not by reusing the old stream reference.

exercises.prompt: This code is supposed to print how many words are longer than 3 letters, and then print the uppercase versions of those same words. Instead, it throws IllegalStateException at runtime. Find and fix the bug.
hints: longWords is a single Stream reference. How many terminal operations does this code call on that same reference?
count() is itself a terminal operation, even though it doesn't look like it 'consumes' anything visually. What happens to a stream once ANY terminal operation has run on it?
You need two SEPARATE streams for two separate pipelines: build one from words.stream() for the count, and a fresh one from words.stream() again for the map-and-collect.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original builds one Stream, longWords, and calls count() on it. count() is a terminal operation, so longWords is consumed once it runs, even though the variable is never reassigned. The next line calls .map(...) on that consumed reference, which throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. The fix starts fresh from words.stream() for each pipeline, one for the count and a new one for the filter-map-collect chain. A stream is a one-shot description of a computation, not a reusable data structure, so each pipeline over the same source needs its own stream.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, in order? Pay attention to what distinct() and sorted() each do, and in which order they run.
hints: distinct() removes duplicates but does not change relative order among the elements it keeps.
sorted() puts elements into ascending order regardless of what order they arrived in.
Trace resultA: remove duplicates from {4,1,4,3,2,1,4} first (keeping first-seen order), THEN sort what's left. Then trace resultB with the two steps swapped. Does the FINAL result end up different?
exercises.expectedAnswer:
[1, 2, 3, 4]
[1, 2, 3, 4]
Both pipelines produce the same final list, even though distinct() and sorted() run in a different order in each: distinct-then-sort and sort-then-distinct happen to agree here because sorting doesn't introduce or remove duplicates, and removing duplicates doesn't disturb sorted order once it's already established.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For resultA: distinct() first reduces {4,1,4,3,2,1,4} to {4,1,3,2} (keeping each value's first occurrence, dropping later repeats), and then sorted() orders that down to [1,2,3,4]. For resultB: sorted() first orders the original list to [1,1,2,3,4,4,4], and then distinct() removes the now-adjacent duplicates, also landing on [1,2,3,4]. Both pipelines print the identical final list. This isn't a coincidence specific to this data: sorting a list never creates or removes duplicate VALUES (it only reorders them), and removing duplicates from an already-sorted list never disturbs the sortedness of what remains, so distinct-then-sort and sort-then-distinct are guaranteed to agree on the final set and order of elements in general, even though the two pipelines do meaningfully different amounts of work to get there (sorting a larger, not-yet-deduplicated list versus a smaller, already-deduplicated one).

options: This code throws an exception immediately, because a Stream cannot be assigned to a variable without a terminal operation.
filter() has already run and produced a filtered Stream containing "bb" and "ccc".
filter() eagerly evaluates and discards "a" right away, but leaves "bb" and "ccc" unprocessed until a terminal operation runs.
filter() has not actually processed any elements yet -- it has only recorded a step in the pipeline.
assessments.explanation: This is stream laziness: intermediate operations like filter build up a pipeline description without processing elements when called, and nothing runs until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, count, and so on) is invoked. The “filter() has already run and produced…” option is wrong because it assumes eager evaluation, which streams do not do. The “This code throws an exception immediately…” option is wrong: assigning an intermediate Stream to a variable with no terminal operation yet attached is completely legal and compiles/runs without any exception; it hasn't done anything yet. The “filter() eagerly evaluates and discards "a" right…” option is a plausible-sounding but incorrect middle ground: filter() does not partially evaluate anything; either the whole pipeline runs, when a terminal operation demands it, or none of it does.

assessments.prompt: Someone on your team says streams are 'just a fancy way to write a for-loop' and doesn't see why laziness or the single-use rule matter in practice. Explain why they actually do matter, with a concrete scenario for each.
assessments.modelAnswer: Streams differ from a for-loop in two ways with observable consequences. First, laziness: none of a stream's intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, and so on) process elements when they are called; they only build up a description of a pipeline. Nothing runs until a terminal operation, like collect or forEach, is invoked, at which point elements are pulled through the whole chain. This matters in two ways: it enables short-circuiting, so an operation like findFirst() or anyMatch() can stop pulling elements through the pipeline the moment it has its answer, without ever touching the rest of a large (or even conceptually infinite) source: something a naive for-loop written by hand would need to replicate manually with a break. It also means that if you build a pipeline and forget to attach a terminal operation at all, the whole thing does nothing at run time, which is a different failure mode from a for-loop, where forgetting to 'finish' the loop isn't really a coherent mistake to make in the same way. It's worth knowing this so an accidentally terminal-operation-less pipeline doesn't get mistaken for a bug somewhere else. Second, the single-use rule: a Stream can be traversed exactly once; once any terminal operation has run on it, that stream is consumed, and calling anything else on that same reference throws IllegalStateException. This is a trap in practice when someone tries to reuse one stream variable for two different purposes (say, counting how many elements match a condition, and then separately collecting the transformed matches into a list) because it's easy to assume a stream behaves like a List you can iterate as many times as you want. The fix is to build a fresh stream, from the same source, for each pipeline you need to run, which is cheap and what streams are designed for, but it does require internalizing that a Stream reference is a one-shot pipeline, not a reusable collection.

assessments.prompt: Stream<String> s = List.of("a", "b").stream(); long count = s.count(); List<String> upper = s.map(String::toUpperCase).collect(Collectors.toList()); What happens on the second statement operating on s?
options: It throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed.
It silently returns an empty list, since the stream's elements were already used up by count() and none remain to map.
It works fine, producing [A, B], since count() only reads from the stream without actually consuming it.
It recomputes the stream from scratch internally, since Stream objects automatically refresh themselves each time a new operation is chained onto them.
assessments.explanation: count() is a terminal operation, even though it superficially looks like a harmless read, and the moment any terminal operation runs, the stream it ran on is considered consumed. Calling .map(...) on that same, already-consumed s reference afterward throws IllegalStateException at run time. The “It works fine, producing [A, B], since…” option is wrong because there is no such thing as a 'read-only,' non-consuming terminal operation in the Stream API: every terminal operation consumes the stream it's called on. The “It silently returns an empty list, since…” option invents a silent-failure behavior Java's streams don't have; the failure is a loud, immediate exception. The “It recomputes the stream from scratch internally…” option describes a self-refreshing behavior streams don't implement: a Stream is an one-shot pipeline over its source, not a renewable view.

assessments.prompt: Optional<Integer> result = Stream.<Integer>empty().reduce((a, b) -> a + b); What does this evaluate to, and why does this form of reduce return an Optional at all rather than an int directly?
options: It returns Optional.of(0), because 0 is used as an implicit default identity value whenever none is explicitly supplied to reduce.

It returns Optional.empty(), because the one-argument reduce overload has no identity value to fall back on for an empty stream, so it has to express 'no result' explicitly rather than inventing an arbitrary answer.

It fails to compile, because reduce can only ever be called with exactly two arguments: an identity value and a combining function, and the version that takes a single argument was removed when Optional was introduced to the language.
It throws NoSuchElementException immediately, because reduce always requires at least one element to combine, empty stream or not.
assessments.explanation: The single-argument reduce(BinaryOperator<T>) overload has no identity value supplied by the caller, so for an empty stream there's no combining to do and no starting value to fall back on and hand back as-is: there is, correctly, no sensible T to return. Rather than picking an arbitrary placeholder, this overload returns Optional<T>, forcing the caller to handle the empty case, and for an empty stream that Optional is empty. The “It throws NoSuchElementException immediately, because reduce always…” option is wrong: reduce does not throw for an empty stream when using this overload; that's the scenario Optional is there to represent safely. The “It returns Optional.of(0), because 0 is used…” option invents a default identity that doesn't exist for this overload; 0 is never assumed. The “It fails to compile, because reduce can…” option is wrong because reduce has multiple legitimate overloads, including this exact one-argument form used here.

assessments.prompt: Which statement accurately distinguishes filter and map from sorted and distinct, in terms of stateless versus stateful stream operations?
options: filter and map are stateful because they each require a Predicate or Function argument, while sorted and distinct take no arguments at all and are therefore stateless.
filter and map are stateful because they can reject or transform elements, while sorted and distinct are stateless because they merely reorder or deduplicate what's already there.

filter and map are stateless -- deciding what to do with one element only ever requires that element's own value, never any knowledge of other elements; sorted and distinct are stateful -- sorted cannot know an element's correct final position until every other element has been seen, and distinct must remember every element it's already emitted.
There is no real distinction between the four operations; all are implemented identically internally and differ only in which lambda is supplied to them.
assessments.explanation: filter and map process each element independently, using only that element's own value: nothing about handling one element depends on having seen any other. sorted, by contrast, cannot place any element into its final position without having compared it against every other element in the stream, and distinct has to remember every distinct value already emitted so far to recognize a later repeat, both depend on more than just the one element currently being processed, which is what makes them stateful. The “filter and map are stateful because they can…” option gets the labels backwards. The “There is no real distinction between…” option is wrong because the stateless/stateful distinction is a, documented property with consequences for buffering and parallel behavior, not a cosmetic difference. The “filter and map are stateful because they each…” option bases the distinction on argument count, which isn't the criterion at all: sorted() can even take a Comparator argument and remains just as stateful.

assessments.prompt: A teammate rewrote a simple loop over 50 orders as a parallel stream with several nested lambdas 'for performance', and now a total sometimes comes out wrong. What went wrong and what would you recommend?
assessments.modelAnswer: Parallel streams split work across threads, so any lambda that mutates shared state, such as adding to an ArrayList or a running total field, causes races and wrong results. For 50 items the overhead of splitting and joining threads also outweighs any gain, so it is likely slower as well as incorrect. Recommend keeping it sequential and side-effect free: compute totals with mapToDouble or reduce, or collect with built-in collectors like Collectors.groupingBy and summingDouble, which are safe even in parallel because they combine partial results. Use BigDecimal for money rather than double. If readability suffers from nested lambdas, extract named methods or keep a plain loop; streams are a tool for clarity, and parallel() should only be used after measuring a bottleneck with large, CPU-bound work.

concepts.title: Optional and Records: Modern Alternatives to Null Checks and Boilerplate
concepts.description: Optional<T> makes 'this might not have a value' part of a method's return type instead of a silent possibility every caller has to remember on their own, and records give a one-line, immutable alternative to the hand-written getters, constructor, equals, hashCode, and toString every plain data class used to need.
learningObjectives: Explain what problem Optional<T> is designed to solve as a return type, compared to returning null.
Use isPresent/isEmpty, map, orElse, orElseGet, and orElseThrow correctly, and explain why calling get() unconditionally is discouraged.
Explain why Optional is intended primarily as a return type, not as a field type or a method parameter type.
Declare a record and explain precisely what the compiler generates for it automatically.
Explain what it means for a record to be implicitly final and unable to extend another class, and how a compact constructor can validate its components.

sections.heading: The Problem With null as 'No Result': Optional<T> Makes Absence Explicit
sections.body:
A method like `findUserById(int id)` might not find anything, because the id might not exist. Returning `null` for that is legal and common, but it makes every caller responsible for remembering to check, with no help from the compiler: `User user = findUserById(id); user.getName();` compiles whether or not a user was found, and if none was, `.getName()` throws `NullPointerException`, often far from where the missing user first mattered. That distance is why tracing an NPE to its root cause in a large codebase is so tedious.

`Optional<T>` changes this: instead of a `User` that might secretly be `null`, the method returns an `Optional<User>`, a small wrapper meaning 'a `User` is present, or it is not', visible in the signature. This doesn't make it *impossible* to mishandle absence (`Optional` still has a `get()` that can throw), but 'no result' becomes part of the type, a much stronger signal to a caller than a bare `User` that is sometimes `null`.

sections.heading: Using Optional Correctly: map, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow
Where Optional Doesn't Belong: Fields, Parameters, and Collections
sections.body: `Optional` was designed as a **return type** for the 'this operation might not produce a result' case: not as a general-purpose replacement for `null` everywhere in a program. Using `Optional<String>` as a class field, or as a constructor or method *parameter* type, is widely discouraged, for a fairly blunt reason: an `Optional`-typed field or parameter can *still itself be null* (nothing prevents `Optional<String> name = null;`), so you haven't eliminated the null-handling problem there: you've just added an extra layer of unwrapping ceremony (`Optional` isn't `Serializable` either, which occasionally matters for fields). Similarly, prefer returning an empty `List<T>` over `Optional<List<T>>` when a collection might have nothing in it: an empty collection already represents 'nothing here' perfectly well, without needing to wrap it in another layer to express the same idea a second time.

sections.heading: Records: Concise, Immutable Data Carriers
sections.body:
Many classes in a Java codebase exist only to hold a fixed set of values together (a coordinate, a range, a result pair), and used to require a constructor, private final fields, accessors, and correct `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()`, written by hand each time. A **record** (Java 16+) generates all of that from one line:

```java
record Point(int x, int y) { }
```

That one declaration gives you private final fields `x` and `y`; a canonical (all-arguments) constructor; public accessors named after the components, `x()` and `y()`, **not** `getX()`/`getY()`; and `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()` based on all components. Two `Point`s built with the same `x` and `y` are `.equals()` and print the same `toString()` (`Point[x=3, y=4]`).

Records are **implicitly final** (no subclass can extend a record) and implicitly extend `java.lang.Record` (so a record cannot extend any other class), though a record is completely free to **implement** interfaces, just like any other class. Once constructed, a record's components can never be reassigned; there are no generated setters of any kind, only the generated accessors.

sections.heading: Compact Constructors and Records' Sharp Edges

examples.title: Optional Instead of null, End to End
examples.explanation: Map.get(id) returns null when the key is missing, so Optional.ofNullable wraps that possibly-null result in an Optional<String> instead of letting a bare null escape findNameById. Then .map(...) runs its lambda only if a name is present; for id 99, which isn't in USERS, map is skipped and orElse's fallback is used, with no null check written by the caller. The map-then-orElse chain reads as 'if present, transform it, otherwise use this default', replacing an if (name != null) { ... } else { ... }.

examples.title: orElse vs orElseGet: When the Default Is Expensive
examples.explanation: present holds a value, so both a and b end up as "actual-value", but they get there differently. present.orElse(expensiveDefault()) evaluates expensiveDefault() as an ordinary method argument BEFORE orElse is called, whether or not present has a value, so "computing expensive default..." prints and the result is thrown away. present.orElseGet(EagerVsLazyDefault::expensiveDefault) passes a Supplier, which orElseGet invokes only if the Optional is empty. Here it is not, so the supplier is never called and the message does not print a second time. That is why orElseGet, not orElse, is the right choice whenever the fallback costs time or resources.

examples.title: A Record vs the Equivalent Hand-Written Class
examples.explanation: The record declaration alone generates private final fields x and y, accessor methods x() and y() (not getX()/getY()), and value-based equals(), hashCode(), and toString(), all of the boilerplate sketched out in the commented equivalent class below it. The compact constructor, public Point { ... }, adds validation logic without repeating the parameter list a second time; the field assignments (this.x = x; this.y = y;) happen automatically right after the compact constructor's own body finishes, so there's no need to write them. p1.equals(p2) is true even though p1 and p2 are two separate objects, because the generated equals() compares the component values (3 and 4 in both), not object identity: the value-based semantics you'd otherwise have to implement by hand, correctly, including a matching hashCode().

misconceptions.description: Since Optional makes the possibility of absence explicit in the type, calling .get() on an Optional is always a safe way to retrieve its value.
misconceptions.clarification: get() throws NoSuchElementException immediately if the Optional is empty: wrapping a value in Optional doesn't make retrieving it automatically safe, it just makes the possibility of absence visible in the method's return type. Calling get() unconditionally, without first checking isPresent() (or, better, without ever calling get() at all and instead using orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, or map/ifPresent), reproduces the same 'forgot to handle the missing case' bug that Optional exists to help prevent, just manifesting as a different exception name than NullPointerException.
misconceptions.fact: get() throws NoSuchElementException immediately if the Optional is empty: wrapping a value in Optional doesn't make retrieving it automatically safe, it just makes the possibility of absence visible in the method's return type.

misconceptions.description: Records are essentially mutable data classes with less boilerplate -- you just don't have to write get/set methods by hand.
misconceptions.clarification: Records are immutable by construction, not merely boilerplate-reduced. Every component becomes a private final field, and the compiler generates only accessors (x(), not getX()) and no setters. A record's state cannot change after construction. If you need a 'changed' version, construct a new record with the updated values, the same pattern used for immutable types like String. (The one caveat is a component that is itself mutable, such as an array or a List: the record cannot stop that object from being modified.)
misconceptions.fact: Records are immutable by construction, not merely boilerplate-reduced.

exercises.prompt: This method looks up a discount code and applies it, but it crashes with NoSuchElementException whenever the code doesn't exist. Find the bug and fix it so a missing code produces a clear, deliberate error instead.
hints: rate.get() throws NoSuchElementException immediately whenever rate is empty. When does CODES.get(code) return null, causing that to happen here?
Rather than calling get() unconditionally, use a method on Optional designed for the 'produce a clear error if absent' case.
orElseThrow(() -> new SomeException("message")) lets you throw a, informative exception instead of relying on Optional's own generic NoSuchElementException.
exercises.solutionExplanation: CODES.get("EXPIRED") returns null because that key isn't in the map, so Optional.ofNullable wraps it into an empty Optional, and the original code's unconditional rate.get() throws NoSuchElementException the moment that happens, with only a generic message that doesn't say which code was the problem. The fix replaces get() with orElseThrow(() -> new NoSuchElementException("Unknown discount code: " + code)), which still throws when the Optional is empty, but with a, specific, informative message instead of Optional's own generic one, and it makes the failure path a design choice rather than an accidental consequence of calling get() without checking. Calling getDiscountRate("SAVE10") still works normally, printing 0.1, since that code IS present in CODES.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? Pay attention to exactly what gets compared, and how, by the record's generated equals() method.
hints: a == b compares object identity, the same == rule that applies to any reference type. Are a and b the same object in memory, or two separate ones?
a.equals(b) uses the record's automatically generated equals(), which compares the component VALUES of x and y, not object identity.
Records also generate a toString() that follows a fixed format: ClassName[component1=value1, component2=value2].
exercises.solutionExplanation: a == b is false because a and b are two separate objects created by two separate new Coordinate(...) calls. == on a reference type always compares object identity, and records don't change that rule at all, only equals() is generated specially. a.equals(b) is true because the record's generated equals() compares the component values (x=5, y=10 in both), and they match. a.equals(c) is false because c has y=11, which differs from a's y=10: even one differing component makes the generated equals() return false. Finally, a's generated toString() follows records' fixed format, printing the class name followed by each component name and value in declaration order: Coordinate[x=5, y=10].

assessments.prompt: Which of the following is generated automatically by declaring `record Money(String currency, long cents) { }`, with no additional code written?
options: Private final fields, getCurrency()/getCents() accessor methods following JavaBean naming, and mutator methods setCurrency()/setCents() for updating the values later.
Private final fields for currency and cents, accessor methods currency() and cents(), and value-based equals(), hashCode(), and toString().
Only a constructor -- accessor methods, equals(), hashCode(), and toString() must still be written by hand.
A mutable class with public fields currency and cents that can be reassigned directly from outside the class.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer lists what a record generates: private final fields for each component, accessor methods named after the components (currency(), cents(), not getCurrency()/getCents()), and equals()/hashCode()/toString() implementations based on all components, with no setters, because records are immutable by design. The “Private final fields, getCurrency()/getCents() accessor methods following…” option is wrong on the accessor naming (records don't use the getX() JavaBean convention) and wrong that setters are generated at all: they never are. The “Only a constructor -- accessor methods, equals()…” option understates what's generated; records produce far more than just a constructor, that's the entire point of using one. The “A mutable class with public fields currency…” option is wrong on every count: record fields are private, not public, and there is no way to reassign a record's components after construction.

assessments.prompt: Explain why Optional is generally recommended as a return type but discouraged as a field type or parameter type, and separately explain what a record's compact constructor is for and what actually happens to the record's fields after it runs.
assessments.modelAnswer: Optional<T> earns its usefulness as a return type for methods where 'no result' is a legitimate, expected outcome: it puts that possibility into the method's signature, which is a much stronger, more visible signal to a caller than a bare T that might secretly be null with no indication of that in the type at all. That value doesn't carry over cleanly to fields or parameters, though, for a fairly reason: an Optional-typed field or parameter can still itself be null: nothing about declaring a field as Optional<String> prevents someone from assigning it null, so you haven't removed the null-handling problem in that context, you've only added an extra unwrapping step (calling .get() or .orElse(...)) on top of a problem that's still there underneath. Optional also isn't designed to be a general-purpose null-replacement: it's meant for the 'method might not produce a result' shape, which return types have and fields/parameters generally don't need in the same way; a field either has a value because the object was constructed with one, or the class's own design should make clear what 'no value' means for that field without introducing another wrapper type to express it. As for records: a compact constructor is written without repeating the record's parameter list, and it exists to add validation or normalization logic to the values being used to construct the record. Critically, it does NOT replace the field assignments, those still happen automatically, but only AFTER the compact constructor's own body finishes running. So a compact constructor's job is purely to check or transform the incoming values (throwing an exception on invalid input, for instance) before the implicit assignment step takes over and sets each private final field to its corresponding parameter's value.

assessments.prompt: Optional<String> present = Optional.of("value"); String result = present.orElse(computeExpensiveDefault()); -- assuming computeExpensiveDefault() has an observable side effect, like printing a message, what happens when this line runs, even though present already holds a value?
options: computeExpensiveDefault() is called and its side effect runs, because orElse's argument is evaluated eagerly as an ordinary method argument before orElse itself is even invoked -- regardless of whether the Optional turns out to be present or empty.
This throws an exception, because orElse cannot legally be called on an Optional that already has a value present.
computeExpensiveDefault() is called, but its side effects are automatically suppressed until Java confirms the Optional is actually empty.
computeExpensiveDefault() is never called at all, since present already has a value and the default is unnecessary.
assessments.explanation: Method arguments in Java are evaluated before the method they're passed to is invoked, with no special exception for orElse, so computeExpensiveDefault() runs, side effects and all, as an ordinary part of evaluating this statement, whether or not present later turns out to have a value. Since present does have a value here, the computed default is discarded once orElse decides it isn't needed, but by then the work (and the side effect) has already happened. The “computeExpensiveDefault() is never called at all, since…” option describes orElseGet's laziness, not orElse's. The “computeExpensiveDefault() is called, but its side effects…” option invents a suppression mechanism Java doesn't have: side effects, once triggered by running code, cannot be selectively undone. The “This throws an exception, because orElse cannot…” option is wrong: orElse is always legal to call regardless of whether the Optional is present or empty; that's the entire point of it being a fallback mechanism.

assessments.prompt: record Buffer(byte[] data) { } Buffer b1 = new Buffer(new byte[]{1, 2, 3}); Buffer b2 = new Buffer(new byte[]{1, 2, 3}); System.out.println(b1.equals(b2)); What prints, and why?
options: true, because byte[] specifically is treated as a value type inside records, unlike in ordinary hand-written classes.
true, because records always generate value-based equals() that compares every component by its actual content, arrays included.

false, because the generated equals() calls Object.equals() on each component, and arrays never override that method from Object -- so an array component is compared by reference identity rather than content, even though b1's and b2's arrays happen to hold identical bytes.
This fails to compile, because array types are not permitted as record components.
assessments.explanation: A record's generated equals() compares components using Object.equals() (and generated hashCode() uses Object.hashCode()) for each one, and arrays never override equals() or hashCode() from Object, so an array component is compared by reference identity, as if you'd compared two plain arrays with == outside of any record at all. b1.data and b2.data are two separate array objects, so even though their contents are identical, b1.equals(b2) is false. The “true, because records always generate value-based equals()…” option overstates records' guarantee: it holds for ordinary components but breaks down for array-typed ones. The “This fails to compile, because array types…” option is wrong: arrays are completely legal record component types; they just don't get the value-equality behavior other component types do. The “true, because byte[] specifically is treated…” option is wrong: there is no special-casing of byte[] or any other array type inside record-generated code; the pitfall applies uniformly to every array-typed component.
